evals.prompt: Sandbox note: this environment has Python but no GPU, no CUDA driver and no network access, and torch may not be importable; do not install anything and do not try to execute the GPU code. My RMSNorm benchmark in /workspace/input/wprof-naive-bench/bench_rmsnorm.py gives numbers that jump around from run to run, and I don't trust them. Rewrite it into /workspace/out/bench_rmsnorm.py so that it measures the op's GPU time properly and reports per-iteration statistics I can put in a perf report. Briefly explain what was wrong with the original.
evals.expected_output: A rewritten benchmark that pre-allocates inputs once, runs ~50 warmup iterations and synchronizes, times ~100 iterations with per-iteration torch.cuda.Event pairs recorded asynchronously, synchronizes once after the loop, and reports mean/median/std/min/max with shape, dtype and device. The explanation names the original anti-patterns: no warmup, perf_counter for GPU time, sync before and after every iteration, allocation inside the loop, mean-only reporting.
assertions: Runs warmup iterations of the op (the skill's default is 50) and synchronizes before any timing starts.
Times the GPU work with CUDA events (torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True) and elapsed_time) instead of time.perf_counter().
Does not call torch.cuda.synchronize() inside the timed loop; events are recorded asynchronously and the code synchronizes once after the loop before reading elapsed times.
Allocates the input/weight tensors (and the events) once before the timing loop instead of on every iteration.
Reports distribution statistics (mean plus median/std/min/max) over a reasonable number of iterations (around 100), not only the mean.
Does not present measured latency numbers as if the script had been run, and does not install packages.

evals.prompt: Sandbox note: this environment has Python but no GPU, no CUDA driver and no network access, and torch may not be importable; do not install anything and do not try to execute the GPU code. Instrument the training loop in /workspace/input/wprof-train-loop/train.py so that it prints per-iteration latency, samples per second and the time spent waiting on the DataLoader, ignoring the startup iterations, plus an average at the end. Write the result to /workspace/out/train_timed.py and tell me how to decide from the output whether data loading is my bottleneck.
evals.expected_output: The loop body is bracketed with torch.cuda.synchronize() + time.perf_counter(); the first few (e.g. 5) iterations are excluded; data time is measured from the end of the previous iteration to the arrival of the next batch; per-iteration lines print iter ms and fps = 32 / iter_seconds, with an average at the end. If data time / iteration time exceeds about 0.2, data loading is the bottleneck.
assertions: Brackets the existing loop body with torch.cuda.synchronize() + time.perf_counter() before and after to measure per-iteration latency.
Excludes a warmup window (the first few iterations) from the reported statistics.
Measures data-loading time separately, as the gap between the end of the previous iteration and the arrival of the next batch from the DataLoader.
Reports throughput in samples/sec derived from the batch size (32) and the measured iteration time, with per-iteration output and a final average.
Explains the decision rule: if data time / iteration time is above roughly 0.2, data loading is a bottleneck.
Leaves the model, loss and optimizer logic unchanged and does not install packages.

evals.prompt: Sandbox note: this environment has Python but no GPU, no CUDA driver and no network access, and torch may not be importable; do not install anything and do not try to execute the GPU code. /workspace/input/wprof-profiler-bw/profile_attention.py is supposed to print the top GPU ops from torch.profiler and the softmax bandwidth as a fraction of the GPU's peak, but on PyTorch 2.5 it dies with AttributeError, and I suspect the bandwidth math is off too.
